intuition: A point's squared distance is x² + y²; taking a square root would not change which point is closer. Keep the closest k points seen so far, with the farthest saved point easy to remove. Replace it only when a closer new point arrives.

Euclidean distance contains a square root, but square root preserves ordering for nonnegative values. Compare x²+y² directly to avoid unnecessary computation and rounding. Store negative squared distances so Python’s min heap behaves as a max heap for the retained group. Include the input index to identify the original point and handle equal-distance heap ordering safely.

Before the heap reaches k entries, accept every point. Afterward replace its root only when the new squared distance is smaller. Ignoring a farther point cannot harm the current closest group. After all inputs, return the original coordinate pairs referenced by the retained indices.
Output order is irrelevant, but coordinates and occurrence counts must be preserved: returning distances or inventing another point at the same distance would not satisfy the contract.

concept.question: Why can the farthest retained point guard a small collection of nearest points?
intuition: Sorting every point uses more work than needed when only a small count is requested. Keep just that many best candidates and expose the worst one among them.

approach: Compute each point’s squared distance from the origin.

concept.correctness: Before the collection fills, every seen point is retained. Once full, it contains the closest requested number among seen points: a new farther point cannot improve it, while a closer point must replace its farthest member. Induction preserves this best-candidate set through the entire scan.
